The given expression is

(By partial fraction)
$\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow 2 x^3+8 x^2-2 x & -2 \\ =\left(2 x^3\right. & \left.-x^2-2 x+1\right)+A\left(x^2-1\right) \\ & +B\left(2 x^2+x-1\right)+C\left(2 x^2-3 x+1\right)\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}-1+A+2 B+2 C & =8 \\ -2+B-3 C & =-2\end{aligned}$

We have,
$\frac{1-\sqrt{3} i}{2}=-\left[\frac{-1+\sqrt{3} i}{2}\right]=-\omega$
and $\frac{1+\sqrt{3} i}{2}=-\left[\frac{-1-\sqrt{3} i}{2}\right]=-\omega^2\therefore \quad\left(\frac{1-\sqrt{3} i}{2}\right)^{2020}+\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{3} i}{2}\right)^{2026}\begin{aligned} & =(-\omega)^{2020}+\left(-\omega^2\right)^{2026} \\ & =\omega^{2020}+\omega^{4052}=\omega+\omega^2=-1\end{aligned}$
Now,
$\begin{aligned} & \sum_{j=1}^6(j+\omega)\left(j+\omega^2\right) \\ & =\sum_{j=1}^6\left(j^2+j \omega^2+j \omega+\omega^3\right) \\ & =\sum_{j=1}^6\left(j^2-j+1\right)=\sum_{j=1}^6 j^2-\sum_{j=1}^6 j+\sum_{j=1}^6 1 \\ & =\frac{6(6+1)(12+1)}{6}-\frac{6(6+1)}{2}+6 \\ & =7 \times 13-3 \times 7+6=91-21+6=76\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \therefore \sin \left(\sum_{j=1}^6(j+\omega)\left(j+\omega^2\right) \frac{3 \pi}{152}\right) & =\sin \left(\frac{76 \times 3 \pi}{152}\right) \\ & =\sin \frac{3 \pi}{2}=-1\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad\left(\frac{1-\sqrt{3} i}{2}\right)^{2020}+ & \left(\frac{1+\sqrt{3} i}{2}\right)^{2026} \\ & +\sin \left(\sum_{j=1}^6(j+\omega)\left(j+\omega^2\right) \frac{3 \pi}{512}\right) \\ =-1-1 & =-2\end{aligned}$

We, have, $P(1, k)$ lies on ellipse
$\begin{aligned} & 9 x^2+4 y^2-18 x+16 y-11=0 \\ & \therefore \quad 9+4 k^2-18+16 k-11=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad 4 k^2+16 k-20=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad k^2+4 k-5=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad(k+5)(k-1)=0 \Rightarrow k=-5,1 \\ & \end{aligned}\therefore P$ is either $(1,-5)$ or $(1,1)$
Again, equation of ellipse is
$\begin{aligned} & & 9 x^2+4 y^2-18 x+16 y-11 & =0 \\ \Rightarrow & & 9(x-1)^2+4(y+2)^2 & =36 \\ \Rightarrow & & \frac{(x-1)^2}{4}+\frac{(y+2)^2}{9} & =0\end{aligned}\therefore$ Eccentricity, $e=\sqrt{1-\frac{a^2}{b^2}}=\sqrt{1-\frac{4}{9}}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\therefore$ Equation of directrices are
$\begin{aligned} y+2 & = \pm \frac{b}{e} \Rightarrow y+2= \pm \frac{9}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \Rightarrow y+2+\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}} & =0 \text { or } y+2-\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}}=0\end{aligned}$
Now, distance of $(1,-5)$ from $y+2+\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}}=0$ is

Distance of $(1,-5)$ from $y+2-\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}}=0$ is $\left|-5+2-\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}}\right|=\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}}+3$
Distance of $(1,1)$ from $y+2+\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}}=0$ is $\left|1+1+\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}}\right|=\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}}+2$
and distance of $(1,1)$ from $y+2-\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}}=0$ is
$\left|1+2-\frac{9}{2 \sqrt{5}}\right|=\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}}-3\therefore$ Shortest distance $=\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}}-3$

questions.solution:
(I) We have,
$\begin{aligned} f(x) & =\sin \left(\cot ^{-1}\left(\cos \left(\tan ^{-1} x\right)\right)\right) \\ & =\sin \cot ^{-1} \cos \cos ^{-1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^2}} \\ & =\sin \cot ^{-1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^2}} \\ & =\sin \sin ^{-1} \sqrt{\frac{1+x^2}{2+x^2}}=\sqrt{\frac{1+x^2}{2+x^2}}\end{aligned}\therefore \quad f(0)=\sqrt{\frac{1+0}{2+0}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
So, Statement $\mathrm{I}$ is false.
(II) We have,
$\begin{aligned} \sin \left(4 \tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{5}-\tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{239}\right) & =\sin \left(2 \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{\frac{2}{5}}{1-\frac{1}{25}}\right)-\tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{239}\right) \\ = & \sin \left(2 \tan ^{-1} \frac{5}{12}-\tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{239}\right) \\ = & \sin \left(\tan ^{-1} \frac{\frac{10}{12}}{1-\frac{25}{144}}-\tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{239}\right) \\ = & \sin \left(\tan ^{-1} \frac{120}{119}-\tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{239}\right) \\ = & \sin \left(\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{119}{1+\frac{120}{119} \times \frac{1}{239}}\right)\right) \\ = & \sin \tan ^{-1}\left[\frac{28680-119}{28441+120}\right]=\sin \tan ^{-1} \frac{28561}{28561} \\ = & \sin \tan ^{-1} 1=\sin \cdot \frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}$
Statement II is false.

Therefore $12(\alpha-\beta)^2=35$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which of the following components of an $L-C-R$ circuit, with an AC supply, dissipates energy?
questions.solution:
In an AC-circuit, the power or rate of energy
dissipated is
$P=V I \cos \phi$
where, $\phi=$ phase difference between voltage and current.
For inductor $(L)$ and capacitor $(C)$, the phase difference between $V$ and $I$ is $90^{\circ}$.
$\therefore \quad P_{L \text { or } C}=V I \cos 90^{\circ}=0 \quad\left(\because \cos 90^{\circ}=0\right)$
For resistor $(R)$, the phase difference between $V$ and $I$ is zero.
Hence, only due to resistor $R$, energy is dissipated in an $L-C-R$ circuit.

questions.solution:
The given situation is as shown in figure,
As, momentum is conserved in collision, $\therefore \quad p_i=p_f\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow & m_1 v_0=m_2 v_2+m_1 \frac{v_0}{3} \\ \Rightarrow & v_2=\frac{2 m_1 v_0}{3 m_2}\end{array} Given that, the bag rises upto height $h$. questions.q:
From a uniform circular disc of radius $2 \mathrm{~cm}$ (its centre of mass is at $O$ ) a circular portion of radius $1 \mathrm{~cm}$ is removed such that the shift in centre of mass is maximum. The disc is
now rotated by an angle $\theta$ about an axis perpendicular to its plane and passing through $O$. If the magnitude of displacement of new centre of mass is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \mathrm{~cm}$, then the $\theta$ is
questions.solution:
The situation given can be shown as,
Here, $R$ be the radius of circular disc $=2 \mathrm{~cm}$ The radius of removed portion, $r=1 \mathrm{~cm}$ Area of whole disc, $A_1=\pi R^2=4 \pi \mathrm{cm}^2$ Area of removed portion, $A_2=\pi r^2=\pi \mathrm{cm}^2$ As, $\frac{1}{4}$ th area of the disc is removed, so remaining area of the disc is $\frac{3}{4}$ th initial area. Similarly, remaining mass, $m_1=\frac{3}{4} m$ Mass of removed portion, $m_2=\frac{1}{4} m$ Let $x$ be the maximum shift in centre of mass. So, initially centre of mass along $X$-axis of complete disc, $\begin{aligned} x_{\mathrm{CM}} & =\frac{m_1 x+m_2 r}{m_1+m_2} \\ 0 & =\frac{\frac{3}{4} m x+\frac{1}{4} m r}{\frac{3}{4} m+\frac{1}{4} m}\end{aligned}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{3}{4} m x=-\frac{1}{4} m r$ or $x=-\frac{1}{3} r=-\frac{1}{3} \mathrm{~cm}$ i.e., the centre of mass of remaining portion will shift to the left of origin at $\frac{1}{3} \mathrm{~cm}$. Now, the disc is rotated by angle $\theta$, so the centre of mass will also shift by angle $\theta$ as shown
$\triangle O P Q$ is isoscales. So, a perpendicular drawn from $O$, on $P Q$ divide the angle $\theta$ and length $P Q$ in equal parts i.e., $R Q=\frac{1}{2} P Q=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \mathrm{cm} \quad\left(\right.$ given, $\left.P Q=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)$ From $\triangle O R Q$, $\begin{array}{rlrl} & & \sin \frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{R Q}{O Q}=\frac{\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}{\frac{1}{3}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad & \sin \frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=\sin 60^{\circ} \\ \Rightarrow \quad & \theta=120^{\circ}\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The modulation index used in amplitude modulation of a message signal of peak voltage $10 \mathrm{~V}$ is 0.5 . By how much the peak voltage of the carrier signal be changed, so as to obtain the modulation index of 0.8 , keeping the peak voltage of the message signal same as before?
questions.solution:
Initially modulation index, $\mu=0.5$ and
message amplitude, $A_m=10 \mathrm{~V}$
As,
$\mu=\frac{A_m}{A_c} \Rightarrow A_{c_1}=\frac{A_m}{\mu}=\frac{10}{0.5}=20 \mathrm{~V}$
When $\mu=0.8$ and $A_m=10 \mathrm{~V}$,
$A_{c_2}=\frac{A_m}{\mu}=\frac{10}{0.8}=12.5 \mathrm{~V}$
Change in carrier amplitude is
$\Delta A_c=A_{c_1}-A_{c_2}=20-12.5=7.5 \mathrm{~V}$
Thus, carrier frequency is reduced by $7.5 \mathrm{~V}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The de-Broglie wavelength of the electron in the first Bohr orbit of the hydrogen atom is
options: equal to the diameter of the first orbit
equal to the circumference of the first orbit
equal to the half circumference of the first orbit
independent of the size of the first orbit
questions.solution:
According to de-Broglie hypothesis, revolving
electron in circular orbit shows wave nature. Hence, a circular orbit can be taken to be a stationary energy state only if it contains an integral number of de-Broglie wavelength, i.e. we must have,
$2 \pi r_n=n \lambda$
where, $r_n=$ radius of $n$th orbit and $n=$ number of stationary state. For first orbit,
$n=1 \Rightarrow 2 \pi r=\lambda$
So, de-Broglie wavelength of the electron in the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen atom is equal to the circumference of first orbit.

questions.q: Consider a parallel plate capacitor which is maintained at potential $200 \mathrm{~V}$. The separation distance between the plates of capacitor and the area of plates are $1 \mathrm{~mm}$ and $20 \mathrm{~cm}^2$, respectively. Calculate displacement current in $1 \mu \mathrm{s}$.
questions.solution:
Displacement current,
$\begin{aligned} I_d & =\varepsilon_0 \frac{d \phi}{d t}=\varepsilon_0 \frac{\Delta \phi}{\Delta t} \\ & =\varepsilon_0 \frac{\Delta E A}{\Delta t} \quad(\because \phi=E \cdot A)\end{aligned}=\frac{\varepsilon_0 \cdot \Delta V \cdot A}{\Delta t \cdot d} \quad\left(\because E=\frac{V}{d}\right)$
Here, $\Delta V=200 \mathrm{~V}$,
$\begin{aligned} \Delta t & =1 \mu \mathrm{s}=10^{-6} \mathrm{~s}, \\ d & =1 \mathrm{~mm}=1 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m} \\ \text { and } \quad A & =20 \mathrm{~cm}^2=20 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}^2\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad I_d & =\frac{8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 200 \times 20 \times 10^{-4}}{10^{-6} \times 10^{-3}} \\ & =3.5 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~A}=3.5 \mathrm{~mA}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Find the acceleration of our galaxy, due to the nearest comparably sized galaxy. The approximate masses of each galaxy is $8 \times 10^{11}$ solar mass and they are separated by 2 million light-years. Each galaxy has a diameter of 100000 light year.
(Assume, 1 light year $\approx 10^{16} \mathrm{~m}$, gravitational constant, $G \approx 10^{-10}\left(\frac{\mathrm{Nm}^2}{\mathrm{~kg}^2}\right)$ and mass of sun $=2.0 \times 10^{30} \mathrm{~kg}$ )
questions.solution:
Here, masses of each galaxy are
$\begin{aligned} m_1 & =m_2=8 \times 10^{11} \text { solar mass } \\ & =8 \times 10^{11} \times 2 \times 10^{30} \mathrm{~kg} \\ & =16 \times 10^{41} \mathrm{~kg}\end{aligned}$
Distance between galaxies is
$\begin{aligned} d & =2 \times 10^6 \text { light year } \\ & =2 \times 10^6 \times 10^{16} \mathrm{~m}=2 \times 10^{22} \mathrm{~m}\end{aligned}$
Force of gravitational pull on each of galaxy is
$F=\frac{G m_1 m_2}{d^2}=\frac{10^{-10} \times\left(16 \times 10^{41}\right)^2}{\left(2 \times 10^{22}\right)^2}$
Acceleration of galaxy is
$\begin{aligned} a & =\frac{F}{m}=\frac{10^{-10} \times\left(16 \times 10^{41}\right)^2}{\left(2 \times 10^{22}\right)^2 \times 16 \times 10^{41}} \\ & =\frac{10^{-10} \times 16 \times 10^{41}}{\left(2 \times 10^{22}\right)^2}=4 \times 10^{-13} \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: In an ideal gas, if the masses of all molecules are doubled and their speeds are halved, then the ratio of initial and final pressures of the gas is
questions.solution:
Pressure of an ideal gas is given by
$p=\frac{1}{3} \frac{m N}{V}\left(\mathbf{v}^2\right)$
When mass of molecule is doubled and speed is halved, pressure becomes
$p^{\prime}=\frac{1}{3} \frac{(2 m) N}{V} \cdot\left(\frac{\mathbf{v}}{2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{2}\left\{\frac{1}{3} \frac{m N}{V}(\mathbf{v})^2\right\}\begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{2} p^{\prime} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \frac{p}{p^{\prime}}=\frac{2}{1} \Rightarrow p: p^{\prime}=2: 1\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
Consider a steady flow of oil in a pipeline. The cross-sectional radius of the pipeline decreases gradually as $r=r_0 e^{-\alpha x}$, where $\alpha=\frac{1}{3} \mathrm{~m}^{-1}$ and $x$ is the distance from the pipeline inlet. If $R_1$ is the Reynold's number
for a certain pipeline cross-section at a distance $x_1$ metre from the inlet and $R_2$ is for distance $\left(x_1+3\right)$ metre, then the ratio $\frac{R_1}{R_2}$ is
questions.solution: Reynold's number of flow is given by $R_e=\frac{2 v \rho r}{\eta}$ where, $v=$ velocity of flow, $\rho=$ density of fluid, $r=$ radius of tube and $\eta=$ viscosity of flow Now, required ratio is $\begin{aligned} & \frac{R_1}{R_2}=\left(\frac{2 v_1 \rho r_1}{\eta}\right) /\left(\frac{2 v_2 \rho r_2}{\eta}\right) \\ & \frac{R_1}{R_2}=\frac{v_1}{v_2} \times \frac{r_1}{r_2}\end{aligned}$ From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $\begin{aligned} \frac{R_1}{R_2} & =\frac{r_2^2}{r_1^2} \times \frac{r_1}{r_2}=\frac{r_2}{r_1} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{R_1}{R_2} & =\frac{r_0 e^{-\alpha\left(x_1+3\right)}}{r_0 e^{-\alpha x_1}}=\frac{e^{-\alpha x_1} \cdot e^{-3 \alpha}}{e^{-\alpha x_1}}=e^{-3 \alpha} \\ & =\frac{1}{e^{3 \alpha}}=\frac{1}{e} \quad\left(\because \alpha=\frac{1}{3} \mathrm{~m}^{-1}\right)\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The average depth of an oil well is $2000 \mathrm{~m}$. If the bulk modulus of oil is $8 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^2$ and the density of oil is $1500 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^3$. The fractional compression at the bottom of the well is (take, $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )
questions.solution:
Bulk modulus is given by
$B=\frac{-p V}{\Delta V} \Rightarrow \frac{-\Delta V}{V}=\frac{p}{B}$
So, fractional compression (in $\%$ ) is
$-\frac{\Delta V}{V} \times 100=\frac{p}{B} \times 100=\frac{\rho g h}{B} \times 100[\because$ where, $p=$ pressure $=\rho g h]\begin{aligned} & \text { Here, } \rho=1500 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m}^{-3} \\ & \qquad \begin{aligned} g & =10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}, \\ h & =2000 \mathrm{~m} \\ B & =8 \times 10^8 \mathrm{Nm}^{-2}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\therefore$ Fractional compression
$=\frac{1500 \times 10 \times 2000}{8 \times 10^8} \times 100=3.75 \%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A projectile is thrown into air with velocity $15 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ at an angle $30^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. After what time its direction of motion is perpendicular to its initial direction? (Assume, $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )
questions.solution:
The given projectile motion is as shown in figure,
Let $t$ be the time after which the initial direction is perpendicular to its direction of motion. As, velocity of a projectile has two components. So, its initial velocity is given by $\mathbf{v}_1=u \cos \theta \hat{\mathbf{i}}+u \sin \theta \hat{\mathbf{j}}$ Since, in projectile motion the horizontal component of velocity remains same, while the vertical component varies, so its velocity after time $t$, $\begin{aligned} & \mathbf{v}_2=u_y \hat{\mathbf{i}}+v_y \hat{\mathbf{j}} \\ & \mathbf{v}_2=u \cos \theta \hat{\mathbf{i}}+(u \sin \theta-g t) \hat{\mathbf{j}}\end{aligned}\left[\because v_y=u_y-g t=u \sin \theta-g t\right] \ldots$ As, velocities are perpendicular, so $\mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}_2=0$ From Eqs (i) and (ii), we get $\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow & (u \cos \theta \dot{\mathbf{i}}+u \sin \theta \mathbf{j}) \cdot(u \cos \theta \mathbf{i}+(u \sin \theta-g t) \mathbf{j})=0 \\ \Rightarrow & u^2 \cos ^2 \theta+u \sin \theta(u \sin \theta-g t)=0 \\ \Rightarrow & u^2 \cos ^2 \theta+u^2 \sin ^2 \theta-u \sin \theta \times g t=0 \\ \Rightarrow & u^2\left(\cos ^2 \theta+\sin ^2 \theta\right)-u g t \sin \theta=0 \\ \Rightarrow & u^2=u g t \sin \theta \quad\left(\because \sin ^2 \theta+\cos ^2 \theta=1\right) \\ \Rightarrow & t=\frac{u}{g \sin \theta}\end{array} Here, $u=15 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}, g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ and $\theta=30^{\circ}\therefore \quad t=\frac{15}{10 \times \sin 30^{\circ}}=\frac{15 \times 2}{10}=3 \mathrm{~s}

questions.q: An object is placed at a certain distance left to a convex lens of focal length $20 \mathrm{~cm}$. Find the distance of the object if the image obtained is magnified by 4 times.
questions.solution: For a lens, Magnification $=\frac{\text { Size of image }}{\text { Size of object }}=\frac{v}{u}\Rightarrow \quad m=\frac{I}{O}=\frac{v}{u}$ Here, $m= \pm 4$ For $m=-4,-4=\frac{v}{u} \Rightarrow v=-4 u$ Now by lens formula, $\begin{array}{rlrl} & & \frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u} & =\frac{1}{f} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{-4 u}-\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{20} \quad(\because f=20 \mathrm{~cm}) \\ \Rightarrow \quad & \frac{-5}{4 u} & =\frac{1}{20} \Rightarrow u=\frac{-5 \times 20}{4}=-25 \mathrm{~cm}\end{array}$ So, object is at a distance of $25 \mathrm{~cm}$ from lens when image is real. For, $m=+4,+4=\frac{v}{u} \Rightarrow v=4 u$ Again from lens formula, $\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u} & =\frac{1}{f} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{4 u}-\frac{1}{u} & =\frac{1}{20} ; \Rightarrow \frac{-3}{4 u}=\frac{1}{20} \\ \text { or } u=\frac{-3}{4} \times 20 & =-15 \mathrm{~cm}\end{aligned}$ So, object is at a distance of $15 \mathrm{~cm}$ from the lens, when image is virtual.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Newton's law of cooling is a special case of
questions.solution:
According to Stefan's law heat energy
absorbed is given by
$\frac{d Q}{d t}=\varepsilon \sigma A\left(T^4-T_0^4\right)$
where, $T=$ temperature of body
and $T_0=$ temperature of surroundings.
If $m$ be the mass of body and $c$ be the specific heat, then heat loss at temperature $T$ is
$\frac{d Q}{d t}=-m c \frac{d T}{d t}$
From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
$\begin{aligned}-m c \frac{d T}{d t} & =\varepsilon \sigma A\left(T^4-T_0^4\right) \\ \Rightarrow \quad-\frac{d T}{d t} & =\frac{\varepsilon \sigma A}{m c}\left(T^4-T_0^4\right)\end{aligned}$
Here, $T=T_0+\Delta T\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad-\frac{d T}{d t} & =\frac{\varepsilon \sigma A}{m c}\left[\left(T_0+\Delta T\right)^4-T_0^4\right] \\ & =\frac{\varepsilon \sigma A}{m c} T_0^4\left[\left(1+\frac{\Delta T}{T_0}\right)^4-1\right] \\ & =\frac{\varepsilon \sigma A}{m c} T_0^4\left[1+\frac{4 \Delta T}{T_0}-1\right] \quad\left(\because \Delta T \ll T_0\right) \\ & =\frac{\varepsilon \sigma A 4 T_0^3}{m c} \Delta T \\ \Rightarrow \quad-\frac{d T}{d t} & =k \Delta T\end{aligned}$
where, $\quad k=\frac{\varepsilon \sigma A 4 T_0^3}{m c}\therefore \quad \frac{d T}{d t}=-k\left(T-T_0\right)$
This is Newton's law of cooling.
Hence, Newton's law of cooling is a special case of Stefan's law.

questions.solution:
Following changes occur in given conversion process
So, required thermal energy $\begin{gathered}=m\left\{c_{\text {ice }}\left(0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}-\left(-10^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)\right)+\right. \\ L_{\text {fusion }}+c_{\text {water }}\left(100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}-0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right) \\ +L_{\text {vapnorisation }} \\ \left.+c_{\text {steam }}\left(110^{\circ} \mathrm{C}-100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)\right\}\end{gathered}\begin{aligned} & =\frac{400}{1000}\{0.5 \times 10+80+1 \times 100+540+0.48 \times 10\} \\ & =29.192 \mathrm{kcal}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Choose the incorrect statement.
options: The fringe width in a Young's double slit experiment reduces when the width between the two slits increases.
The central fringe observed for in a single slit diffraction experiment is a bright fringe.
The resolving power of the microscope is reciprocal to the maximum separation of two points seen as distinct.
Polarisation phenomenon is observed only for transverse waves.
questions.solution:
(a) In Young's double slit experiment, the
fringe width is given by
$\beta=\frac{\lambda D}{d} \Rightarrow \beta \propto \frac{1}{d}$
So, if width between two slit $(d)$ increases, the fringe width reduces.
(b) In diffraction due to single slit, the path difference between rays reaching centre of screen is zero, so its intensity at centre is maximum i.e., bright fringe is observed at centre.
(c) The resolving power of microscope is
$=\frac{1}{d_{\min }}=\frac{2 n \sin \beta}{1.22 \lambda}$
So, it is the reciprocal of the minimum separation $\left(d_{\min }\right)$ of two points seen as distinct.
(d) The polarisation is possible only in those waves, that have vibrations in different direction, which is in case of transverse waves. Hence, only statement given in option (c) is incorrect.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An engine sounding a whistle of frequency $2000 \mathrm{~Hz}$ is receding from the stationary observer at $72 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h}$. What is the apparent frequency of the observer? The velocity of sound in air is $340 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.
questions.solution: Here a source is moving away from a stationary observer. So, frequency recorded at source will be lower than true frequency. Apparent frequency at observer, $f^{\prime}=f\left(\frac{v}{v+v_s}\right)$ where, $v=$ speed of sound $=340 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ and $v_s=72 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h}=72 \times \frac{5}{18}=20 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}\therefore \quad f^{\prime}=2000\left(\frac{340}{340+20}\right)$ Hence, $\quad f^{\prime}=1889 \mathrm{~Hz}$
